newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP urges sale of some oil reserves.
newsitem.headline: German FDP urges sale of some oil reserves.

text.p: Germany should sell part of its crude-oil reserves to help reduce its budget deficit, Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of the Free Democrats, said on Wednesday.

Germany holds a 124-day supply of crude oil in reserve, while the law requires only 90 days. A reduction of even 20 days would bring the government 1.5 billion marks ($866.3 million) in revenue, Westerwelle said in a radio interview.

"The state only shrinks in response to the pressure of problems," said Westerwelle, whose party is the junior partner in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition and stands for lower taxes and a slimmer government.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel has been searching every nook and cranny of the budget for opportunities to cut spending or increase revenues, in a bid to narrow the budget deficit and qualify for European monetary union.
His efforts led to an unusually open and bitter split with the Bundesbank in the past few weeks over a plan to revalue the central bank's gold and foreign reserves.
Waigel told parliament on Wednesday he had reached an agreement with the Bundesbank to transfer windfall revaluation profits to Bonn starting in 1998.
Westerwelle said a 20-day reduction in Germany's oil reserves would also reduce annual storage costs by 20 million marks, and free up storage capacity that the government could rent out.
The budget must be consolidated without tax increases, he said. The government should closely examine all of 430 enterprises it owns to determine which could be privatised.
"Many people have no idea how much belongs to the federal government and what all the government believes it must own," he said.
Westerwelle acknowledged that the open battle between the government and the central bank had damaged the coalition. "Now we must win back trust," he said.
-- Terence Gallagher, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 ($ = 1.731 German Marks)
